title: AQ Khan: How to Live Dangerously
summary: Josh and Chuck profile A.Q. Khan, the Pakistani metallurgist who worked on uranium enrichment at a Dutch company, returned to Pakistan to lead its uranium bomb program, and then ran a clandestine nuclear proliferation network supplying centrifuges and designs to Iran, North Korea, and Libya. The episode covers his early life, the Dutch surveillance, Pakistan's 1970s bomb effort, the Iran, North Korea and Libya deals, the 2003 BBC China shipment seizure, the US-Pakistan Cold War and post-9/11 politics that shielded him, his house arrest and pardon, his hero status in Pakistan, and his death from COVID-19 in 2021. A short listener mail about Branford, Ontario's famous residents closes the show.

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Hosts open the show and introduce the episode on A.Q. Khan.

segments.title: Khan's early life and Dutch enrichment job
segments.summary: Khan is born in India in 1936, moves to West Pakistan, earns metallurgy degrees, and works in the Netherlands at a uranium enrichment firm supplying Urenco, where Dutch intelligence begins monitoring his questions and snooping.

segments.title: Enrichment versus plutonium science
segments.summary: Chuck explains that bombs can be made from enriched uranium or plutonium, and how centrifuges separate uranium isotopes.

segments.title: 1971 war and Khan's letter to Bhutto
segments.summary: Pakistan's humiliating 1971 war with India motivates Khan, who writes to Prime Minister Bhutto proposing a bomb built on uranium rather than plutonium. Bhutto meets him, and Khan plans to gather supplier information from his Dutch job.

segments.title: Stealing blueprints and leaving the Dutch firm
segments.summary: Khan copies blueprints and supplier lists at work. The Dutch move him off enrichment projects in 1975 and he leaves the company in December 1975 with sensitive documents.

segments.title: Project 706 and first highly enriched uranium
segments.summary: Back in Pakistan Khan leads the uranium project, Project 706, amid rivalry with Munir Ahmad Khan, and by 1982 Pakistan produces small amounts of highly enriched uranium.

segments.title: Nuclear energy as cover and the NPT
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how countries pursue nuclear energy while also seeking weapons, and how the 1960s nonproliferation treaty is weakly enforced.

segments.title: Khan's side business and Iran centrifuge sales
segments.summary: Khan builds a smuggling and export side business and sells centrifuges to Iran starting in 1987, including P-1 and P-2 types, with the belief that early shipments were outdated equipment.

segments.title: Iran's bomb pursuit, Iraq, and bargain prices
segments.summary: Chuck discusses why Iran's program has been slow, citing a fatwa against nukes, and the hosts cover Khan's dealings with Iraq, including a suspicious sample and a five million dollar offer with a ten percent commission. Iran reportedly found cheaper suppliers.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: North Korea, the 1998 test, and Libya's centrifuge deals
segments.summary: North Korea turns to Khan after a 1990s deal with the US, with Khan visiting North Korea at least thirteen times. A North Korean delegation attends Pakistan's 1998 test, a woman in the delegation is killed, and missile technology flows from North Korea to Pakistan. Khan's next client is Libya in the late 1990s, through a Dubai partner and a network of middlemen, and a 2003 shipment on the BBC China was intercepted.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: BBC China seizure and Pakistan's US ties
segments.summary: The BBC China shipment exposes the network. US pressure follows, with Musharraf removing Khan from the labs, and the US tolerating Pakistan because of its Cold War and Afghanistan roles, including Congressional certification ties to military aid.

segments.title: Libya deal, Khan's confession, house arrest and pardon
segments.summary: Gaddafi gives up his nuclear program in December 2003 and blames Khan. Khan confesses on TV, is put under house arrest, and is pardoned. Pakistan blocks direct IAEA and CIA access to him, and the US accepts this in exchange for Iranian secrets.

segments.title: US-Iran history and presidential blame
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck argue that the roots of US-Iran nuclear issues go back decades, with multiple administrations involved, including Carter, Reagan and George H. W. Bush.

segments.title: Khan's later years and hero status in Pakistan
segments.summary: Khan is fully released in 2009 and is restricted from interviews. He is hailed as a hero in Pakistan, having argued that Muslim countries should have nuclear weapons, and the hosts note the patriotism and money that motivated him.

segments.title: Khan's wealth, hotel, and death
segments.summary: Khan's estimated wealth is about four hundred million dollars, and he owned a hotel in Timbuktu. He died in October 2021 of COVID-19 and received a military funeral.

segments.title: Khan's survival and plutonium irony
segments.summary: Chuck remarks that Khan lived to old age without being assassinated, and notes that North Korea and Pakistan later relied more on plutonium than the centrifuge route Khan favored.

segments.title: Adam Curtis and Gaddafi's image
segments.summary: Chuck recommends Adam Curtis's documentary Hypernormalization, which argues Gaddafi was a US punching bag, and the hosts joke about Gaddafi's aviators and perm.

segments.title: Listener mail: Branford, Ontario
segments.summary: Listener Jay notes that Alexander Graham Bell was born in Branford, Ontario, more famous than Wayne Gretzky or Phil Hartman. Chuck agrees.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck gives the email address and Josh closes the show.
